title: 'Can't Handle H-1B Visa Stress Anymore': NRI Techie Plans Return to India After Eight Years in the US
excerpt: A tech worker's anonymous Reddit post about abandoning the American dream after five years on H-1B and three on OPT has struck a nerve with thousands of Indians wrestling with the same decision.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • An NRI tech worker plans to return to India after eight years in the US due to visa stress.
  • Chronic visa-related stress and lack of savings prompted the decision to leave the US.
  • Commenters suggest ₹4-5 crore in savings for a comfortable return to India.
  • Experiences of returning Indians vary, with some thriving and others facing adjustment challenges.
  • 34% of Indian-origin tech workers in the US considered returning to India in 2025.
  • An NRI tech worker posted on Reddit about plans to return to India in April after spending eight years in the US — five on H-1B and three on OPT
  • The worker cited chronic visa-related stress, lack of savings, and inability to plan long-term as reasons for leaving
  • The post triggered a debate about the financial threshold needed to return comfortably, with some suggesting ₹4-5 crore in liquid assets
  • Reddit users who have made the reverse move shared mixed experiences, with some thriving and others struggling to readjust

An anonymous tech worker's post on Reddit has gone viral within the Indian diaspora community, capturing a sentiment that many H-1B holders feel but few articulate publicly: the American dream, for some, isn't worth the visa stress.

The Post

Writing on a popular NRI subreddit, the user described spending over eight years in the US — three on OPT (Optional Practical Training, the post-graduation work authorisation) followed by five on H-1B — before deciding to return to India next April. The reasons were blunt: chronic stress from visa uncertainty, no meaningful savings despite years of work, and a growing realisation that long-term planning was impossible when your right to remain in the country depended on employer sponsorship.

"I can't handle the H-1B visa stress anymore," the user wrote. "I'm single, I have no savings to show for 8 years here, and I don't want to do a regular 9-to-5 back in India either. But at least I'll be able to breathe."

The Financial Debate

The post triggered an extensive discussion about the financial realities of returning to India. Several commenters argued that returning without substantial savings was risky, with multiple users citing ₹4-5 crore (approximately $475,000-$600,000) in liquid assets as the minimum needed for a comfortable transition — accounting for the salary differential, lifestyle adjustment, and the need for a financial cushion while re-establishing a career.

Others pushed back, arguing that the fixation on a magic number was itself a symptom of the anxiety the original poster was trying to escape. "People returned to India with nothing 20 years ago and built careers," one commenter wrote. "The India you're going back to in 2026 has more opportunity than the one most of our parents left."

"I can't handle the H-1B visa stress anymore. I'm single, I have no savings to show for 8 years here, and I don't want to do a regular 9-to-5 back in India either. But at least I'll be able to breathe."

— Anonymous NRI on Reddit

The Broader Pattern

The post resonates because it reflects a broader shift. While official data on "reverse migration" is limited, anecdotal evidence and survey data suggest an increasing number of Indian tech workers in the US are seriously considering or actively planning returns to India — driven by a combination of H-1B backlogs (the wait for an employment-based green card for Indian nationals now exceeds 50 years in some categories), rising anti-immigrant sentiment, and India's improving economic opportunities.

A 2025 survey by the National Association of Software and Service Companies (NASSCOM) found that 34% of Indian-origin tech workers in the US had "actively considered" returning to India in the previous 12 months, up from 22% in 2023.

The Adjustment Challenge

Those who have made the move shared mixed experiences. Some described thriving in India's startup ecosystem, enjoying lower costs and closer family ties. Others warned about the "reverse culture shock" — adjusting to different workplace norms, dealing with bureaucracy, and reconciling the India they remembered with the one they returned to.

For the thousands of Indian H-1B holders reading the thread, the post is less a how-to guide than a mirror — reflecting a decision that many are quietly weighing every time a visa renewal comes due.
